stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Musicologist Ines Arroyo traces one of the stranger reversals in the history of Western dance music. The chaconne—imported to Spain from the Americas around 1600, sung with bawdy refrains, and condemned by clerics, who tried to ban it from Madrid's theaters ______ within a century, slowed into the solemn variation form that Bach would later use in his Partita in D minor.
explanation: The interruption that describes the chaconne opens with a dash right after "The chaconne," so it has to close with a dash too. Remove everything between the dashes and you get "The chaconne was, within a century, slowed into the solemn variation form..." That is a complete sentence. The comma inside the phrase, before "who," opens the relative clause, and that clause ends where the dash interruption ends. The closing dash therefore finishes both at once, and the main verb "was" follows with no conjunction.

B.why: You saw the comma before "who" and closed the most recent element with a matching comma, so you lost track of the dash that opened the interruption much earlier. The dash is never closed, which leaves an interruption opened with a dash and closed with a comma. The marks at the two ends of an interruption must match.

C.why: A semicolon needs a complete sentence on each side. "The chaconne—imported ... theaters" has no main verb, and "was, within a century, slowed..." has no subject, so both sides are fragments.

D.why: You closed the dash correctly, but then you added "and," which treats the sentence as if it joins two things. Nothing comes before "was" for "and" to join it to: "The chaconne" has no earlier main verb. Removing the interruption leaves "The chaconne and was slowed...," which is not grammatical.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Immunologists long assumed that the adult immune system could do without its earliest training ground. The thymus, an organ that, in most people, reaches its greatest size at puberty and is then slowly replaced by fat ______ to produce small numbers of new T cells well into middle age, according to a 2024 imaging study of 300 volunteers.
explanation: The appositive "an organ that ... replaced by fat" opens with the comma after "The thymus" and has to close with a comma after "fat." Leave the commas around "in most people" alone, because they belong to a smaller interruption inside the appositive. The word "however" then gets its own pair of commas. Cross out both interruptions and you get "The thymus continues to produce small numbers of new T cells..." That is a complete sentence, with "thymus" as the subject and "continues" as its verb.

B.why: You saw "however" and automatically put a semicolon before it. Adding "it" makes the text after the semicolon a complete sentence, so that side passes the test. The text before it does not: "The thymus, an organ that ... replaced by fat" has no main verb. A semicolon cannot follow a fragment.

C.why: You left the appositive unclosed. It opened with a comma after "The thymus," so it needs a matching comma after "fat." Without that comma, "however" runs into the appositive and the sentence never clearly returns to its subject.

D.why: You added "and," which makes "continues" read as a second verb joined to "reaches" and "is replaced" inside the appositive. The subject "The thymus" is then left with no main verb, and the appositive never gets its closing comma.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Musicologists have long struggled to date the works of nineteenth-century composers who rarely signed or dated their scores. For the Danish composer Ingrid Vestergaard, help came from an unexpected source. Her diaries, which record not only her compositions but also the concerts she attended, the visitors she received, and the weather of each ______ allowed researchers to place nearly forty undated pieces in sequence.
explanation: The comma after "diaries" opens a nonessential which-clause. That clause runs through "the weather of each day," so it has to be closed with a matching comma before the main verb "have allowed." The commas inside the list are part of the clause, so they don't close it. Cross out the clause and you get "Her diaries have allowed researchers to place nearly forty undated pieces in sequence."

A.why: You closed the clause, but adding "and" turns "have allowed" into a second verb of the which-clause ("which record... and have allowed"). That leaves "Her diaries" with no main verb, so the sentence is a fragment.

B.why: You may have counted a list comma as the closing mark. The which-clause opened with a comma after "diaries" and is never closed, so the clause runs straight into the main verb.

D.why: You put a semicolon after a fragment. "Her diaries, which record...each day" has no main verb and can't stand alone, so the semicolon has no complete sentence on its left.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Neptune's gravity can account for the orbits of most objects in the outer solar system. Sedna is an exception. Sedna, a remote icy body on an orbit so elongated that a single circuit of the Sun ______ never comes close enough to Neptune to have been flung outward by it. Some astronomers have therefore proposed that a passing star pulled it into its present path.
explanation: The comma after "Sedna" opens an appositive that runs to "11,000 years." A matching comma has to close it before the main verb "never comes." Nothing inside the appositive needs punctuation: "takes roughly 11,000 years" is a plain verb followed by its object. Remove the appositive and you get "Sedna never comes close enough..."

B.why: You put commas inside the phrase, splitting "takes" from its object, and you never closed the appositive before "never comes."

C.why: You left the appositive open. Without a closing comma, the extra description runs straight into the main verb "never comes."

D.why: You correctly closed the appositive but also added a comma after "takes." That comma pairs with the closing one and walls off "roughly 11,000 years" as if it were removable, which cuts the verb off from its object.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Off the western Aleutian Islands, sea otter numbers collapsed in the 1990s, probably because killer whales began hunting them. The effects spread through the whole food web. Having lost nearly all of the sea otters, the predators that had kept urchin grazing in ______ region's kelp forests were reduced to barren rock within a decade.
explanation: The sentence opens with an introductory participial phrase. That phrase contains its own appositive ("the predators that had kept urchin grazing in check") renaming "the sea otters." The comma after "otters" opens that appositive and doesn't hand off to the subject. The real handoff comes after "check," where the main subject "the region's kelp forests" begins, so you need one comma there.

A.why: You read the comma after "otters" as the handoff to the subject and left the introductory phrase open. Without a comma after "check," the appositive runs into the main subject.

C.why: You put a semicolon after a fragment. Everything before the blank is an introductory phrase with no subject or main verb, so it can't stand alone.

D.why: Adding "and" makes it look as if two complete thoughts are being joined. The text before the blank is only a modifying phrase, so there is nothing for "and" to join it to.

stimulus: The immune system must destroy invaders while sparing the body's own cells. Tolerance, the system's capacity—maintained largely by a small population of regulatory T cells—to leave healthy tissue ______ down in autoimmune diseases such as type 1 diabetes, in which immune cells attack the pancreas's insulin-producing cells.
explanation: There are two interrupters. The inner one is the dash pair around "maintained largely by...T cells," and it is already closed. The outer one is the appositive opened by the comma after "Tolerance," and it runs to "unharmed." Because a comma opened it, a comma has to close it, right before the main verb "breaks."

A.why: You matched the nearest mark, the dash, instead of the mark that opened this interrupter. The appositive began with a comma after "Tolerance," so it must close with a comma. The dash pair is already complete.

B.why: You left the appositive open, so the extra description runs straight into the main verb "breaks."

C.why: You closed the appositive but then joined it to a new clause with "and." "Tolerance, the system's capacity..." has no verb of its own, so "and" links a fragment to a sentence.

The list commas belong to the clause. The clause opened with a comma, so a comma after "bracelet" closes it before the main verb "was."

C.why: You closed the interrupter with a different mark from the one that opened it. A clause opened with a comma has to close with a comma, not a dash.

D.why: You put a semicolon after a fragment. "The hoard, which..." never gets a main verb before the semicolon, so the left side can't stand alone.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Whole grains and legumes are often recommended as dietary sources of iron and zinc. Phytate, a compound that plants use to store phosphorus, concentrated in the bran and hulls of those same ______ binds both minerals in the gut and can sharply reduce how much of them the body absorbs. Soaking, sprouting, and fermenting these foods break down much of it.
explanation: The comma after "Phytate" opens an appositive that runs to "foods." The appositive needs a closing comma before the rest of the main clause. "However" then sits inside the main clause as an interrupting adverb, so it also needs commas on both sides. The comma after "foods" does both jobs: it closes the appositive and opens "however."

A.why: You treated "however" as if it began a new sentence. The text before the semicolon ("Phytate, a compound...foods") has no main verb and can't stand alone.

C.why: With no comma after "foods," "however" falls inside the appositive, and the appositive is never properly closed before the verb "binds."

D.why: You correctly closed the appositive but stopped there. "However" interrupts the main clause, so it needs a comma after it as well. Otherwise it runs into "binds."

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Storm surges in the estuary have grown steadily higher over the past thirty years. The new floodgate's design, which its engineers, drawing on tide-gauge records from every major storm since 1990, revised twice before construction ______ the steel barrier to rise from the riverbed in under twenty minutes.
explanation: The comma after "design" opens a nonessential which-clause. Inside it is a second interrupter, "drawing on tide-gauge records...since 1990," which is set off by its own pair of commas. The which-clause continues through "revised twice before construction began," so it needs a closing comma right before the main verb "allows." Remove the clause and you get "The new floodgate's design allows the steel barrier to rise..."

A.why: You may have taken the comma after "1990" as the end of the which-clause. That comma only closes the inner phrase, so the outer clause is still open when it reaches "allows."

B.why: You closed the clause but added "and it," as though two complete thoughts were being joined. "The new floodgate's design, which..." has no main verb, so the first part is a fragment.

C.why: You put a semicolon after a fragment. Everything before the blank is a subject plus a modifying clause, with no main verb, so it can't stand alone.
